shots.title: War Is Over!
shots.sub: THE FALSE ARMISTICE · WHAT THE PAPERS PRINTED · NOVEMBER 1918
shots.say: War is over. That is what the Seattle Star told its readers on Thursday, November seventh, nineteen eighteen. There was just one problem. The war was not over. It would go on for four more days.

Paris, November seventh, by United Press leased wire. The allies and Germany signed an armistice at eleven o'clock this morning. Hostilities cease at two o'clock this afternoon. A place, a time, and a news agency behind it. It read like the most solid news of the war.

In Kansas, the Topeka State Journal rushed out a third war extra. Reports of Hun surrender. Armistice with Germany is signed at eleven o'clock this morning, ending the world's greatest war. But look at the end of that line. A question mark.
In Hammond, Indiana, the Lake County Times did not hedge at all. Hostilities ceased at two o'clock. War ends.

From Seattle to Indiana, front pages printed the end of the First World War. People poured into the streets. And by that evening, the whole story had fallen apart. So where did the news come from? Who sent it? And why did so many papers believe it? The answer was waiting in a French port on the Atlantic coast.

shots.title: The flash
shots.say: Part one. The flash.

The Topeka paper printed who stood behind the story. It is true, United Press. The bulletin which brought the first news to America of the signing of the armistice was signed personally by Roy W. Howard, president of the United Press.

This is Roy Howard, photographed in nineteen fourteen. Four years later he was running the United Press, one of the biggest news wires in America, and he was in France. A bulletin with his own name on it was not a rumor. It was a guarantee.
Papers raced to get it out. In South Bend, Indiana, the News-Times set its headline so fast that it misspelled the word itself. Armisitce is signed. Hostilities cease at once.

Underneath, the paper added a second source. From New York: the report that an armistice has been signed is a Wall Street report, but is guaranteed to be absolutely reliable, by the Dow, Jones and Company financial news agency. Wall Street and the Stock Exchange are in mid air in consequence, particularly since Washington declines official confirmation.
Washington declines official confirmation. Buried at the end of a paragraph, it was the first crack in the story. And it was about to get much wider.

shots.title: New York goes wild
shots.say: Part two. New York goes wild.
Topeka's front page tracked the celebration city by city. Washington is wild. Celebrate in Chi. New York goes wild. Broadway crazy after news of surrender is spread.

A New York report printed in Omaha the next day described it. Sophisticated New York became delirious with joy today over the unfounded report that Germany had agreed to armistice terms. The celebration seemed a combination of Fourth of July, election night, New Year's eve, Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Back in Hammond, the Times made its own speed part of the story. Country mad with jubilation. United Press scoops all news collecting agencies all over the United States.

Across the top of the page, the Times congratulated itself. Times extra gives first real news. For a newspaper, a scoop is the best thing that can happen. Unless it turns out to be wrong. And on that same page, there was already a warning.

shots.title: The denial
shots.say: Part three. The denial.
In the middle of the Hammond front page, below the flag and the words war ends: State Department had no confirmation at two p.m.

Topeka printed the same doubt, right below Howard's bulletin. Doubt on reports. It was officially announced at the state department at two fifteen o'clock this afternoon that the Germans had not signed armistice terms. The word not, in capital letters, on the same page as Germans beaten.

In Oklahoma City, the Times, on Associated Press wire, ran the story the other way round. Early unofficial reports that armistice had been signed officially denied by Secretary Lansing, after cable inquiries to French capital. Rejoicing is premature.
In El Paso, Texas, the Herald said it outright. Report armistice is signed officially denied by U.S.

Secretary of State Robert Lansing explained how he knew. When the report reached his department that morning, an inquiry was sent to Paris. At two oh four in the afternoon, the reply came back. The armistice had not been signed. And the German representatives would not even meet Marshal Foch until five p.m., Paris time.
The German envoys had not even sat down at the table. So where had the United Press found a signed armistice? The answer came the next morning, and it came from the Navy.

shots.title: The admiral
shots.say: Part four. The admiral.

On Friday, New York's Evening World printed it. Admiral Wilson assumes responsibility for report that armistice was signed. Commander at Brest says the information appeared to be official, and exonerates United Press.

This is Henry B. Wilson, photographed a few years later, in nineteen twenty three. In November nineteen eighteen, he was the admiral commanding the American forces in French waters, at the port of Brest. That is where Roy Howard was on Thursday.

The admiral's statement: The statement of the United Press relative to the signing of the armistice was made public from my office, on the basis of what appeared to be official and authoritative information.

I am in a position to know that the United Press and its representative acted in perfect good faith, and that the premature announcement was the result of an error for which the agency was in no wise responsible.

card.label: EDWARD HOUSE, PARIS · 8 NOV 1918
card.note: "It is perfectly clear that United Press was not at fault in this matter."
card.source: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1918, Supp. 1, Vol. I, doc. 404

shots.say: In Paris, the President's special representative, Edward House, looked into it. In a telegram to Washington on November eighth, he traced the report to a wire from the American naval attaché in Paris to Admiral Wilson at Brest. Wilson showed it to Howard, and Howard's dispatch got past the cable censor. House wrote: It is perfectly clear that United Press was not at fault in this matter. The blame, he said, lay with the attaché, or with the French official who began the rumor.
Its great rival, the Associated Press, was less forgiving. In Omaha, the Bee printed the verdict. Armistice report is greatest hoax of recent years.
And next to it: Whole country duped by false news of peace.

The same front page held a clue to how a rumor like this could start. Fighting stopped on one sector of western front, to permit passage of Germany's armistice envoys. A pause in the guns. Not the end of the war.
Because the war was still going on. Friday's Evening World said so across the whole page. Foch won't stop fighting. Must take terms by Monday.

shots.title: Monday
shots.say: Part five. Monday.

card.label: EDWARD HOUSE TO THE PRESIDENT
card.note: "Armistice signed 5 o'clock this morning. Hostilities to cease 11 a.m. today."
card.source: FRUS 1918, Supp. 1, Vol. I, doc. 417 · 11 November 1918

shots.say: Early on Monday, November eleventh, the real telegram came. Edward House cabled the President from Paris. Armistice signed five o'clock this morning. Hostilities to cease eleven a.m. today.
That afternoon, the Evening World printed it. Foch calls off fighting. Thousands of U.S. guns fire their last shots at eleven a.m.

And New York celebrated again. Bain News Service photographers were in the streets that Monday. Look at the edge of this glass plate. Someone wrote the caption by hand. Peace hurrah. Eleven, eleven, eighteen.
A parade, with flags and a man in a top hat, past a crowd on the sidewalk. People in the windows above, watching.
A street of tall buildings, hung with flags, and packed from wall to wall. This time, the news was true.
In Seattle, the Star put out an eighth extra. Armistice is signed. War ends. Four days earlier, the same newspaper had told the same readers: war is over.

b.label: EDWARD HOUSE TO THE PRESIDENT · THE RECORD

shots.say: Printed: an armistice signed on Thursday, November seventh. The record: an armistice signed at five in the morning on Monday, November eleventh. Four days apart.

So the papers that Thursday did not invent a peace. They had a bulletin signed by the head of a news wire, released from an American admiral's office, and passed by a censor. Every link in the chain looked solid. Nobody had checked the first one. If you had read war is over on that Thursday, would you have gone out into the street? Tell me in the comments.
If you like stories told from the papers themselves, give this video a like, and subscribe to As Printed, for what the papers said, and what the archive says.
War is over! That is a real front page, printed on November seventh, nineteen eighteen. But the war was not over.
So who sent it? The bulletin was signed by Roy Howard, president of the United Press, in France.
Papers rushed it out so fast that in South Bend, they misspelled the word armistice.
By that afternoon, Secretary of State Robert Lansing denied it. The German envoys had not even met the Allies yet.
The source? Admiral Henry Wilson at Brest. He said it came from his office, on what appeared to be official information.
The real armistice was signed on November eleventh. Four days after the papers said: war is over.
